title: English Vocabulary 3 · Units 79–80
description: Curated English idioms, multi-word expressions, British pronunciation contrasts, silent letters and word-stress patterns, with original examples and Brazilian Portuguese translations.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. Lexical targets and phonological contrasts are source-based; teaching examples and usage notes are independently written, and original exercises, extended passages and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Checked the study pages and exercises 79.1–79.5 and 80.1–80.7, including the relevant answer-key entries and pronunciation remarks.
audit.pronunciation: Broad standard southern British IPA where confident; potential accent or stress variants explained in notes. Uncertain transcriptions omitted rather than guessed. Longer idioms intentionally omit IPA.
audit.languagePolicy: All content is English except the Brazilian Portuguese translations in pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Compared teaching-page targets and exercises with the answer key; reviewed idiom grammar, spelling, British stress, silent letters, original examples, unique IDs, schema and conservative audio targets.
audit.limitations: No bundled audio, live VocabLab browser import, browser TTS or speech-recognition test was performed.

units.title: Unit 79 — Multi-word expressions
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 79. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Learn idioms as complete phrases with their typical grammatical patterns and register.
Distinguish expressions for misunderstandings, feelings, behaviour and everyday actions.
Use fixed expressions with verbs such as get, make and take naturally in context.
Recognise exercise-only idioms such as hit the sack, fit as a fiddle and once in a blue moon.

sectionsChecked: A: Learning and remembering multi-word expressions

items.example: I felt under the weather, so I stayed home instead of going to the party.
items.note: Informal: usually feel or be under the weather; it means slightly unwell, not a reference to the weather.

items.pt: já teve dias melhores; está desgastado
items.example: My old office chair has seen better days, but it still works.
items.note: Usually used about ageing or worn objects; the expression is conventionally used in a perfect form such as has seen better days.

items.word: take the weight off your feet
items.pt: sentar-se para descansar; descansar as pernas
items.example: You've been standing for hours; come and take the weight off your feet.
items.note: Informal invitation to sit down; too familiar for some formal contexts.

items.word: get the wrong end of the stick
items.section: B · Expressions with a verb and object
items.example: I think you've got the wrong end of the stick: the deadline is next Monday, not tomorrow.
items.note: Usually get the wrong end of the stick; get hold of the wrong end of the stick is an alternative.

items.section: B · Expressions with a verb and object
items.example: The seller tried to pull a fast one by hiding the car's damage.
items.note: Informal: deliberately trick someone; often pull a fast one on someone.

items.pt: intrometer-se em; meter o nariz em
items.section: B · Expressions with a verb and object
items.example: Please don't poke your nose into matters that don't concern you.
items.note: Informal, disapproving: poke your nose into someone else's business or affairs.

items.example: She was over the moon when she heard that she'd won the scholarship.
items.note: Informal: be over the moon about something; means extremely delighted.

items.example: He's been down in the dumps since his football team lost the final.
items.note: Informal: feel or be down in the dumps; usually temporary unhappiness.

items.example: Our department was in the red at the end of the financial year.
items.note: Usually be in the red; describes a negative financial balance or a loss.

items.example: I can be as daft as a brush when I'm tired and forget my keys.
items.note: Informal British English; a playful or critical way to say someone is very silly.

items.pt: ser o cúmulo; passar dos limites
items.example: I've heard plenty of excuses, but that one really takes the biscuit.
items.note: Informal British English: something is the most surprising, annoying or extreme example.

items.pt: um pé no saco; uma pessoa ou coisa irritante
items.example: This paperwork is a pain in the neck when you're trying to finish quickly.
items.note: Informal: an irritating person, task or situation; a pain in the neck, not pain of the neck.

items.example: The children were as good as gold throughout the long journey.
items.note: Often used to praise a child's behaviour; not about financial value.

items.word: make a meal out of it
items.pt: fazer tempestade em copo d'água; exagerar um problema
items.example: The error was minor, but he managed to make a meal out of it.
items.note: Informal: make a meal out of something means treat a simple issue as unnecessarily complicated.

items.example: It's getting late, so we'd better make a move.
items.note: Informal: often make a move means leave; in another context it can mean begin to take action.

items.pt: interesseiro; em busca de ganho próprio
items.example: She avoids doing business with anyone who seems to be on the make.
items.note: Informal, disapproving: seeking money, advantage or power for oneself.

items.pt: complicar algo simples; avançar com dificuldade desnecessária
items.example: I made heavy weather of the report because I kept changing the format.
items.note: British English: make heavy weather of something means make slow, difficult progress unnecessarily.

items.pt: procurando a solução no lugar errado; seguindo uma pista falsa
items.section: C · Fixed grammar and continuous forms
items.example: The engineers are barking up the wrong tree if they blame the network for this mechanical fault.
items.note: The idiom is normally used with be and an -ing form: be barking up the wrong tree.

items.example: I'm exhausted after the trip, so I'm going to hit the sack.
items.note: Informal: go to bed; not a literal action involving a sack.

items.example: That maths exercise is kid's stuff compared with the final exam.
items.note: Informal: something very easy; also written kids' stuff in some contexts.

items.pt: em ótima forma; com saúde de ferro
items.example: After several months of swimming, my grandfather feels fit as a fiddle.
items.note: Informal: extremely healthy or physically fit.

items.pt: tratar com frieza; ignorar de propósito
items.example: I don't know why she's giving me the cold shoulder at work.
items.note: Usually give someone the cold shoulder; intentionally act unfriendly or ignore them.

items.pt: muito raramente; uma vez na vida e outra na morte
items.example: We eat at that expensive restaurant only once in a blue moon.
items.note: Informal: very rarely; often used to describe an infrequent repeated event.

items.pt: pegar o jeito; aprender a fazer
items.example: The software seemed confusing, but I soon got the hang of it.
items.note: Informal: understand how to use or do something; often get the hang of something.

units.title: Unit 80 — Words commonly mispronounced
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 80. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Recognise common British English vowel spelling-to-sound contrasts.
Pronounce words with silent p, b, l, h, t and k and recognise non-rhotic British r.
Distinguish common noun–verb stress pairs using short pronounceable word targets.
Notice stress shifts in derived word families and avoid common pronunciation errors.
Practise the rhyme and odd-one-out contrasts from the exercises without relying on spelling alone.

items.section: A · Vowel contrasts and unpredictable spellings
items.example: The cat fell asleep on my backpack.
items.note: The letter a has /æ/ here, contrasting with its sound in late or last.

items.section: A · Vowel contrasts and unpredictable spellings
items.example: Let's talk about the plan after lunch.
items.note: Initial unstressed a is pronounced /ə/ (schwa).

items.section: A · Vowel contrasts and unpredictable spellings
items.example: We wandered around the old town for an hour.
items.note: In standard southern British pronunciation, a sounds /ɒ/ here.

items.section: A · Vowel contrasts and unpredictable spellings
items.example: This is the last train of the evening.
items.note: In the book's British accent, a is /ɑː/; some accents use /æ/.

items.section: A · Vowel contrasts and unpredictable spellings
items.example: The bus arrived late because of heavy traffic.
items.note: The letter a represents the diphthong /eɪ/.

items.section: A · Vowel contrasts and unpredictable spellings
items.example: I met her at the conference last summer.
items.note: Short e is /e/, unlike the long vowel in metre.

items.section: A · Vowel contrasts and unpredictable spellings
items.example: The electricity meter is next to the kitchen door.
items.note: The book illustrates /iː/ in meter; British English normally spells the length unit metre, but measuring devices are meters.

items.section: A · Vowel contrasts and unpredictable spellings
items.example: All the plants were still alive after our holiday.
items.note: The stressed i is /aɪ/ rather than /ɪ/.

items.section: A · Vowel contrasts and unpredictable spellings
items.example: Could you give me a hand with these boxes?
items.note: Although written with i-e, the vowel is short /ɪ/.

items.section: A · Vowel contrasts and unpredictable spellings
items.example: I'm sorry I missed your call.
items.note: Standard British English usually has /ɒ/ in the first syllable.

items.section: A · Vowel contrasts and unpredictable spellings
items.example: We usually go to the library after class.
items.note: The written o is pronounced /əʊ/ in standard British English.

items.section: A · Vowel contrasts and unpredictable spellings
items.example: I love working on practical engineering problems.
items.note: The written o corresponds to /ʌ/.

items.section: A · Vowel contrasts and unpredictable spellings
items.example: We walked to the station together.
items.note: The strong form is /tuː/; normal connected speech often uses /tə/.

items.section: A · Vowel contrasts and unpredictable spellings
items.example: Please put the files in the shared folder.
items.note: The letter u is pronounced /ʊ/, not /ʌ/.

items.section: A · Vowel contrasts and unpredictable spellings
items.example: Please cut the cardboard carefully.
items.note: The letter u is pronounced /ʌ/.

items.section: A · Vowel contrasts and unpredictable spellings
items.example: The painting shows Cupid holding a bow.
items.note: The first syllable starts with /kjuː/, not /kʊ/.

items.section: A · Vowel contrasts and unpredictable spellings
items.example: He nodded his head in agreement.
items.note: The spelling ea is pronounced /e/.

items.section: A · Vowel contrasts and unpredictable spellings
items.example: Our team presented the results yesterday.
items.note: The spelling ea is pronounced /iː/.

items.section: A · Vowel contrasts and unpredictable spellings
items.example: A friend helped me prepare for the interview.
items.note: The spelling ie represents /e/, not /iː/.

items.section: A · Vowel contrasts and unpredictable spellings
items.example: She has always been interested in science.
items.note: The vowel pattern includes /aɪ/ followed by a weak syllable.

items.section: A · Vowel contrasts and unpredictable spellings
items.example: Our flight leaves early tomorrow.
items.note: British English permits /aʊə/ and other reduced pronunciations.

items.section: A · Vowel contrasts and unpredictable spellings
items.example: We chose a different route to avoid traffic.
items.note: Common British pronunciation /ruːt/; /raʊt/ also occurs in English.

items.section: A · Vowel contrasts and unpredictable spellings
items.example: I would prefer to leave before six.
items.note: The spelling ou corresponds to /ʊ/; the l is silent.

items.section: A · Vowel contrasts and unpredictable spellings
items.example: Keep a firm hold on the horse's reins.
items.note: In rein, ei is pronounced /eɪ/.

items.section: A · Vowel contrasts and unpredictable spellings
items.example: Did you receive my revised document?
items.note: In receive, ei represents /iː/.

items.section: A · Vowel contrasts and unpredictable spellings
items.example: The room stayed cool throughout the afternoon.
items.note: The spelling oo is /uː/.

items.section: A · Vowel contrasts and unpredictable spellings
items.example: I usually cook dinner at home.
items.note: The spelling oo is /ʊ/.

items.example: The film features a psychic who claims to predict the future.
items.note: The initial p is silent; the word begins with /s/.

items.example: The university offers research opportunities in psychiatry.
items.note: The initial p is silent; stress falls on /kaɪ/.

items.example: The machine uses a pneumatic actuator to move the valve.
items.note: The initial p is silent; British /njuː/ begins the word.

items.example: Please keep the receipt in case you need a refund.
items.note: The p is silent, even though receipt contains the written letters p and t.

items.example: The novelist publishes under a pseudonym.
items.note: The initial p is silent; British English commonly begins /sjuː/.

items.example: She chose to study psychology at university.
items.note: The initial p is silent, and the main stress is on the second syllable.

items.example: I couldn't find my comb this morning.
items.note: Final b is silent.

items.example: That was a dumb mistake, but we fixed it quickly.
items.note: Final b is silent; dumb can sound offensive when applied to people.

items.example: My fingers went numb in the freezing wind.
items.note: Final b is silent.

items.example: Archaeologists discovered a sealed tomb.
items.note: Final b is silent, and the vowel is /uː/.

items.example: We had to climb three flights of stairs.
items.note: Final b is silent.

items.example: The baby develops in the womb.
items.note: Final b is silent; the vowel is /uː/.

items.example: We ordered lamb with roasted vegetables.
items.note: Final b is silent.

items.example: I doubt that the train will arrive on time.
items.note: The b is silent in doubt and doubtful.

items.example: The changes to the design were quite subtle.
items.note: The b is silent.

items.example: She worked hard to pay off her student debt.
items.note: The b is silent in debt and debtor.

items.example: The company contacted the debtor about the unpaid invoice.
items.note: The b is silent.

items.example: We could test the prototype tomorrow.
items.note: The l is silent.

items.example: You should back up the files before updating the system.
items.note: The l is silent.

items.example: Try to stay calm during the interview.
items.note: The l is not pronounced in the book's standard British pronunciation.

items.example: We finished half the work before lunch.
items.note: The l is silent in standard British English.

items.example: We need to talk about the test results.
items.note: The l is silent.

items.example: She held the small screw in the palm of her hand.
items.note: The l is silent in the common British pronunciation.

items.example: We like to walk to the office when the weather is good.
items.note: The l is silent.

items.example: The restaurant serves grilled salmon.
items.note: The l is silent.

items.example: The teacher wrote the formula in chalk.
items.note: The l is silent.

items.example: It was an honour to receive the award.
items.note: Initial h is silent; British spelling honour.

items.example: She made an honourable decision despite the pressure.
items.note: Initial h is silent; British spelling honourable.

items.example: Please give me an honest opinion of my draft.
items.note: Initial h is silent: an honest opinion, not a honest opinion.

items.example: The repair took less than an hour.
items.note: Initial h is silent; the word begins with a vowel sound.

items.pt: por hora; de hora em hora
items.example: Trains leave the station on an hourly basis.
items.note: Initial h is silent.

items.example: The eldest son became heir to the estate.
items.note: Initial h is silent; use an heir.

items.example: The heiress donated much of her fortune to charity.
items.note: Initial h is silent.

items.example: He began to whistle while washing the dishes.
items.note: The t is silent.

items.example: We visited a medieval castle on the coast.
items.note: The t is silent in standard British English.

items.example: Please listen carefully to the instructions.
items.note: The t is silent.

items.example: Please fasten your seat belt before take-off.
items.note: The t is usually silent.

items.example: A warm cloth can soften the dried glue.
items.note: The t is usually silent; some speakers pronounce it.

items.example: We're visiting our family at Christmas.
items.note: The t in the written -stmas- cluster is silent.

items.example: He injured his knee while running.
items.note: The initial k is silent.

items.example: Please use a sharp knife to cut the vegetables.
items.note: The initial k is silent.

items.example: Do you know when the meeting starts?
items.note: The initial k is silent.

items.example: Turn the knob clockwise to increase the volume.
items.note: The initial k is silent.

items.example: Practical knowledge is important in this job.
items.note: The initial k is silent.

items.example: I tied a knot at the end of the rope.
items.note: The initial k is silent.

items.example: My grandmother taught me to knit.
items.note: The initial k is silent.

items.example: You need an access card to enter the laboratory.
items.note: In standard non-rhotic British English, r is not sounded before another consonant.

items.example: We walked through the park before dinner.
items.note: The r is usually not pronounced in standard non-rhotic British English.

items.example: Her grandparents own a small farm.
items.note: Non-rhotic British English does not sound r before m here.

items.example: Be careful not to burn your fingers.
items.note: The written r colours the vowel but is not a separate consonant in the book's accent.

items.example: She has to work late tonight.
items.note: The r is not pronounced as a consonant in non-rhotic British English.

items.example: A storm damaged several trees near the road.
items.note: The r is not a separate consonant in non-rhotic British English.

items.example: We shared a lemon tart for dessert.
items.note: The r before t is silent in non-rhotic British English.

items.example: My mother is learning English too.
items.note: Final r is normally absent in non-rhotic British English, unless linked to a following vowel in connected speech.

items.example: My sister works at a school nearby.
items.note: Final r is normally silent in non-rhotic British English.

items.example: The teacher explained the problem again.
items.note: Final r is normally silent in non-rhotic British English.

items.example: Could I have a glass of water, please?
items.note: Final r is normally silent in non-rhotic British English.

items.example: She entered a contest to win a place on the course.
items.note: Noun: CONtest, with first-syllable stress.

items.example: The lawyer plans to contest the decision in court.
items.note: Verb: conTEST, with second-syllable stress.

items.example: The factory separates each reject from the items that pass inspection.
items.note: Noun: REject, with first-syllable stress; often refers to rejected products.

items.example: The committee decided to reject the proposal.
items.note: Verb: reJECT, with second-syllable stress.

items.example: Public transport is cheaper than driving into the city.
items.note: Noun: TRANsport, with first-syllable stress.

items.example: Special equipment is needed to transport the fragile samples.
items.note: Verb: transPORT, with later stress in the book's contrast; some accents vary.

items.example: The technician kept a record of every measurement.
items.note: Noun: primary stress on the first syllable, RECORD; contrast to record.

items.example: We need to record the measurements before switching off.
items.note: Verb: primary stress on the second syllable, reCORD.

items.example: Her transfer to another department was approved.
items.note: Noun: typically first-syllable stress, TRANSfer, in the contrast taught here.

items.example: You can transfer the data using a USB cable.
items.note: Verb: the teaching contrast is stress on the second syllable; some speakers vary.

items.example: The police questioned a suspect after the theft.
items.note: Noun: stress SUSpect; a person believed to have committed a crime.

items.example: I suspect that the battery is faulty.
items.note: Verb: stress susPECT.

items.example: The conflict delayed the negotiations.
items.note: Noun: first syllable stressed; compare the verb conflict.

items.example: The results appear to conflict with the earlier study.
items.note: Verb: second syllable stressed; normally conflict with something.

items.example: The school prepared a conduct report for each pupil.
items.note: Conduct as a noun has first-syllable stress, CONduct; typically behaviour or management.

items.example: They plan to conduct another experiment next week.
items.note: Verb: second syllable stressed, conDUCT.

items.example: Visitors must obtain a permit before entering the site.
items.note: Noun: stress PERmit.

items.example: The rules do not permit visitors to enter this room.
items.note: Verb: stress perMIT; formal alternative to allow.

items.example: There was a decrease in equipment costs this year.
items.note: Noun: often DEcrease, with first-syllable stress.

items.example: We expect energy consumption to decrease over time.
items.note: Verb: stress deCREASE.

items.example: The department reported an increase in orders.
items.note: Noun: first syllable stressed, INcrease.

items.example: We need to increase the sampling frequency.
items.note: Verb: second syllable stressed, inCREASE.

items.example: The new tariff applies to every import in this category.
items.note: Noun: first syllable stressed, IMport.

items.example: The application can import data from a text file.
items.note: Verb: second syllable stressed, imPORT.

items.example: Coffee is an important export for the country.
items.note: Noun: first syllable stressed, EXport.

items.example: You can export the results as a CSV file.
items.note: Verb: second syllable stressed, exPORT.

items.example: A peaceful protest took place outside the building.
items.note: Noun: usually first syllable stressed in the teaching contrast.

items.example: Students decided to protest against the proposed change.
items.note: Verb: the book teaches a shift to later stress; actual usage varies by accent.

items.example: She bought a present for her friend's birthday.
items.note: Noun: PREsent is a gift; also an adjective meaning current.

items.example: The researchers will present their findings on Friday.
items.note: Verb: preSENT, with second-syllable stress.

items.example: His remark sounded like an insult.
items.note: Noun: INsult, with first-syllable stress.

items.example: I did not mean to insult anyone with my comment.
items.note: Verb: inSULT, with second-syllable stress.

items.example: Many animals survive in the desert.
items.note: Noun: first-syllable stress, DEsert, with /e/ in the first syllable.

items.example: The soldiers were ordered not to desert their posts.
items.note: Verb: second-syllable stress and /ɜː/ in the stressed vowel.

items.example: We made steady progress throughout the project.
items.note: Noun: usually PROgress in British English.

items.example: We hope to progress to the next stage soon.
items.note: Verb: typically proGRESS in the contrast illustrated in the book.

items.example: The unexpected result caused quite an upset.
items.note: Noun: initial stress, UPset; not the same as the verb upset.

items.example: I didn't want to upset her by mentioning the problem.
items.note: Verb: stress on the second syllable, upSET.

items.section: C · Stress shifts within word families
items.example: The article included a photograph of the new bridge.
items.note: First-syllable stress; contrast photography and photographer.

items.section: C · Stress shifts within word families
items.example: She is taking an evening course in photography.
items.note: The stress moves to the second syllable.

items.section: C · Stress shifts within word families
items.example: The photographer arrived before the ceremony.
items.note: The stress falls on the second syllable.

items.section: C · Stress shifts within word families
items.example: The damage was documented photographically.
items.note: The main stress is later in the word than in photograph.

items.section: C · Stress shifts within word families
items.example: Please keep your telephone switched off in the theatre.
items.note: Initial syllable stress.

items.section: C · Stress shifts within word families
items.example: The company develops services for internet telephony.
items.note: Stress changes compared with telephone.

items.section: C · Stress shifts within word families
items.example: She found arithmetic easier than geometry.
items.note: Stress falls on the second syllable in this noun; pronunciation patterns vary with derivation.

items.section: C · Stress shifts within word families
items.example: The software checks for arithmetical errors.
items.note: The main stress shifts to the syllable containing met.

items.section: C · Stress shifts within word families
items.example: A skilled arithmetician can spot mistakes in complex calculations.
items.note: Derived from arithmetic; note the stress shift before the -ian ending.

items.section: C · Stress shifts within word families
items.example: He plans to study zoology at university.
items.note: The stress pattern in this family changes with longer derivatives.

items.section: C · Stress shifts within word families
items.example: The zoologist studied marine mammals.
items.note: Related to zoology, with a similar stressed vowel.

items.section: C · Stress shifts within word families
items.example: The species is included in several zoological surveys.
items.note: Suffix -ical shifts the primary stress to the later syllable.

items.section: C · Stress shifts within word families
items.example: The psychologist discussed the study results.
items.note: Initial p is silent; the second syllable is stressed.

items.section: C · Stress shifts within word families
items.example: The training had a positive psychological effect.
items.note: Initial p is silent; the stress shifts relative to psychologist.

items.section: C · Stress shifts within word families
items.example: He works in a psychiatric hospital.
items.note: Initial p is silent; the stress shifts relative to psychiatry.

items.section: C · Stress shifts within word families
items.example: The hospital hired a new psychiatrist.
items.note: Initial p is silent; this is a person noun derived from psychiatry.

items.example: Don't forget the apostrophe in the contraction.
items.note: Four syllables; primary stress on the second.

items.example: The flood caused an environmental catastrophe.
items.note: The ending -phe is pronounced /fi/; primary stress on the second syllable.

items.example: The plates are in the cupboard above the sink.
items.note: The p is silent; the word is pronounced with two syllables rather than as cup-board.

items.example: My favourite recipe uses fresh tomatoes.
items.note: Three syllables; final written e is not silent.

items.example: We bought fresh vegetables at the market.
items.note: Commonly four written vowel groups but compressed to about three spoken syllables.

items.example: The museum displays a medieval sword.
items.note: The w is silent; the vowel is /ɔː/ in standard British English.

items.example: You ought to check the details before signing.
items.note: The letters gh are silent; pronounced /ɔːt/.

items.example: The exercise strengthened his leg muscles.
items.note: The c is silent; do not pronounce it as /k/.

items.example: She made an interesting observation.
items.note: Often pronounced with a reduced middle syllable in British English.

items.example: I tend to worry about things I cannot control.
items.note: In British English, the first vowel is /ʌ/, unlike sorry and lorry.

items.example: A large lorry blocked the narrow road.

items.example: Look up the word in a learner's dictionary.

items.example: He tied the equipment with a strong cord.
items.note: The vowel is /ɔː/ in standard British English.

items.example: The observatory has a large glass dome.
items.note: The vowel is /əʊ/, unlike come and some.

items.example: We still have some time before the train leaves.
items.note: The written o is /ʌ/, not /əʊ/.

items.example: She had to plead for more time to finish the work.
items.note: The letters ea represent /iː/, unlike head and tread.

items.example: Please tread carefully on the wet floor.
items.note: The ea is /e/, unlike in plead.

items.example: Please don't shout across the room.
items.note: The ou represents /aʊ/, unlike in could.

items.example: He couldn't stop coughing during the presentation.
items.note: The spelling ough sounds /ɒf/ in standard British English.

items.example: The sea was too rough for swimming.
items.note: The ough is /ʌf/, unlike cough.

items.example: It was a tough decision to make.
items.note: The ough is /ʌf/, as in rough.

items.example: The magician waved a wand over the box.
items.note: The vowel is /ɒ/ in the book's British accent, unlike land and sand.

items.example: The plane is scheduled to land at noon.
items.note: The written a is /æ/, unlike in wand.

items.example: The plant's roots reached deep into the soil.
items.note: The spelling oo usually sounds /uː/ here.

items.example: A layer of soot covered the fireplace.
items.note: Common British pronunciation /sʊt/, unlike root; some variants exist.

items.example: She hurt her foot during the hike.
items.note: The oo is /ʊ/, not the /uː/ of root.

items.example: The farmer used a tractor to plough the field.
items.note: British spelling plough, pronounced with /aʊ/; rhymes with now.

items.example: We walked through the tunnel.
items.note: The ough represents /uː/ and gh is silent; rhymes with who.

items.example: The road was wet, though it had stopped raining.
items.note: The ough represents /əʊ/; rhymes with go.

items.example: We have enough time to run another test.
items.note: The ough sounds /ʌf/; rhymes with stuff.

items.example: He took a clean handkerchief from his pocket.
items.note: The word is normally pronounced with three syllables.

items.example: The laboratory stores each chemical in a labelled container.
items.note: Initial ch is pronounced /k/, not /tʃ/.

items.example: The engineer measured the height of the platform.
items.note: The spelling eigh is /aɪ/; final gh is silent.
